key_insight: The paper turns short-range-order alloy design into a differentiable optimization problem, enabling direct gradient-based search from target SRO to target properties.
engineering_relevance: This provides a faster, scalable route to design high-entropy alloys with tuned stiffness and more realistic thermodynamic behavior than random-swap reverse Monte Carlo.
method: Treat atom occupancy as continuous variables so SRO matching can be optimized with gradient descent.
Add a physics-based thermodynamic correction to keep generated structures realistic across many elements.
Train a small neural network to map composition and SRO statistics to mechanical properties, closing the design loop.
evidence_signal: Across nine FCC and BCC alloys, the approach reproduced SRO-driven stiffness shifts from -20% to +57%, was about 6x faster and 8x more accurate on 4000-atom systems, and matched 3 of 4 Co-Cr-Ni target stiffness values within 6%.
watch_item: Property predictions depend on sufficiently large cells; the abstract notes that 108-atom cells can mislead and that at least 864 atoms are needed to capture the direction and magnitude of SRO-driven changes reliably.
paper_title: Differentiable inverse design of short-range order in high-entropy alloys: from target sro to target property
